archetype.name: Lost Season (defense-first)
archetype.definition: A Harbaugh team whose year is effectively gone at 0-6: the defense is still good enough to keep games within reach, but the offense is too broken to win them.

report.headline: A top-ten defense chained to the league's worst offense, and 0-6 to show.
report.take:
These are not the Chargers of the last two years. Harbaugh's 2024 team allowed the fewest points in the league, and his 2025 team won 11 games behind a defense ranked 6th in EPA allowed. The defense has mostly held its level: 10th in EPA allowed, 7th against the pass, 6th on third down. The offense, already a weak spot last year (23rd in EPA), has collapsed to dead last in EPA per play, last in pass EPA and 31st in success rate. The worst point differential in the league, -10.2 a game, is almost entirely the offense's doing.

The root is the protection. The line ranks 31st in sack rate and last in QB hit rate, and it also commits more penalties than any other line in the league. Justin Herbert has taken 21 sacks in six starts, and the offense has turned it over 15 times. The staff has responded by running more than any team in football relative to the situation (-11.4 pass rate over expected, 32nd), but the run game sits 30th in EPA, so the conservative plan protects nothing and gains little. This isn't the schedule, either. Arizona and Las Vegas beat them in L.A. as 8.5- and 6.5-point underdogs, and those defenses now rank 27th and 22nd. The passing has gotten worse as the season has gone on, ending with -14 pass EPA in the 22-6 loss at Kansas City.

Two things in the numbers flatter the team's failures. The 25.2 points allowed a game, 22nd, overstates what the defense is doing; 15 giveaways hand opponents short fields that EPA allowed doesn't punish the defense for. The record is also worse than the play. The differential implies 2.6 wins, they've lost every close game, and Wins Over Expected ranks them last at -2.62. That still makes them a bad team that has been unlucky, not a good team in disguise. Injuries count too. Joe Alt has played four games and Derwin James three, and both are questionable again.

With Kansas City at 5-1 and Denver at 5-2, the division is gone, and the rest of the year is about whether the offense can become functional. The bye, a Rams defensive front missing three regulars, and soft spots against Houston, the Jets and Miami give them chances to break the winless run. A defense this sound should steal a few games. An offense this bad caps how many.

strengths.title: Pass defense that still travels
strengths.body: The coverage and the pass rush together rank 7th in pass EPA allowed and 9th on short throws, and opponents convert only 31.1% on third down. This group carried the team the last two years, so it is the most reliable part of the roster. It has held up even with Derwin James in and out.

strengths.title: Pressure that turns into takeaways
strengths.body: The sack total is middling, but the defense hits quarterbacks at the 5th-highest rate and has 10 takeaways, 7th in the league. Five of those came in one game at Buffalo, so the rate will cool. The hits are real, though, and they keep giving a dead offense extra possessions.

strengths.title: A record worse than the play
strengths.body: The point differential implies 2.6 wins, not zero, and they haven't won a single one-score game. Close-game results swing back toward even over a season, so a few of the coin flips should start landing their way. That points to a team that can win some games, not one that can climb back into the race.

concerns.title: Protection has sunk the passing game
concerns.body: A 9.5% sack rate (31st) and the league's worst QB hit rate have produced the league's worst pass EPA. The problem is structural. It shows up against good and bad defenses alike, and the line also leads the league in penalties. Getting Alt back would help, but one tackle doesn't fix a unit this far down.

concerns.title: Giveaways hand away games
concerns.body: Fifteen turnovers in six games, including four at Seattle and three in each loss to Las Vegas and Denver. These swamp a defense that is forcing turnovers at a top-ten rate. Some of it is fumble and tipped-ball randomness, but a pressured quarterback behind a leaky line will keep giving the ball away more than most.

concerns.title: Running a lot, running badly
concerns.body: No team leans further away from the pass than this one, yet the run game ranks 30th in EPA with a 35% success rate. The heavy run rate looks like a way to hide the protection, but it leaves the offense in long down-and-distance with Herbert under fire. The plan needs to change, not just its execution.

trend.note: The passing game has gotten steadily worse, from roughly neutral against Las Vegas to -10.3 pass EPA against Denver and -14 in the 6-point showing at Kansas City. The bye is the first real chance to reset.

nextGame.headline: Off a bye, a broken offense meets a depleted Rams front
nextGame.body:
The Rams are 3-4 but play like a much better team: 6th in net EPA, 1st in yards per game, with a line that allows pressure at the 2nd-lowest rate and leads the league in stuff rate. Like the Chargers, they've been unlucky, with -1.59 Wins Over Expected. Their weak spots fit what the Chargers need. The pass rush is 27th in pressure rate and 28th in sack rate, the takeaway count is low, and the special teams are the league's worst by EPA. The Book has the Rams -6.5 with a total of 44.5, the Chargers +230, indoors.

Availability favors the visitors' protection. The Rams have Kobie Turner and Poona Ford on injured reserve, Myles Garrett is on IR awaiting a possible practice window next week, linebacker Nate Landman is out with a concussion, and Trent McDuffie sat out the last game with a groin injury. On the Chargers' side, Joe Alt, Derwin James, guard Kayode Awosika, and receivers Tre Harris and Ladd McConkey are all questionable after the bye. McConkey was spotted at practice in a no-contact jersey. How many of those players suit up decides whether this offense looks any different.

waysToWin.title: Finally keep Herbert clean
waysToWin.body: This is the softest pass rush they've seen. It already ranked near the bottom and is now missing Turner and Ford inside. With Alt back and two weeks to rework the plan, the Chargers can throw on early downs instead of running into long third downs. A game with two sacks or fewer gives Herbert a real chance to move the ball.

waysToWin.title: Win the turnover margin outright
waysToWin.body: The Rams are -0.7 a game in turnover margin and have forced only six takeaways. That's a rare chance for the Chargers to play a clean game while their own ball-hawking defense, 7th in takeaways, works on Stafford. A plus-two day erases most of the talent gap the spread implies.

waysToWin.title: Steal field position on special teams
waysToWin.body: The Rams give away -3.86 EPA a game on special teams, the league's worst. For an offense that struggles to drive the length of the field, a short field from a return or a missed kick is the likeliest way to score. The Chargers aren't good on special teams either, but here they hold the edge.

waysToLose.title: Rams run game bleeds the clock
waysToLose.body: The Rams' line leads the league in stuff rate and ranks 5th in run success, while the Chargers allow the 6th-highest rate of explosive runs. If the Rams stay on schedule on the ground, the Chargers' good pass defense never gets the long-yardage downs it feeds on, and their offense gets few possessions.

waysToLose.title: Drives stall short of touchdowns
waysToLose.body: The Rams are 5th on both third down and red-zone touchdown rate, and 2nd against deep throws. An offense 31st in success rate has no easy way past that. Field goals and punts against an offense this productive lose by more than a touchdown.

waysToLose.title: Same self-inflicted damage
waysToLose.body: Nine penalties a game and a giveaway habit have decided several of these losses, including 130 penalty yards and four turnovers at Seattle. If the bye didn't fix the discipline, the Chargers will give back whatever edges the matchup offers.

nextGame.watch: The Chargers' sack and pressure count against a Rams front missing Turner and Ford. If Herbert gets time here and still can't move the ball, the problem goes beyond the line.

restOfSeason.body:
The defense is the part to trust: its pass-defense and third-down numbers match the last two seasons, so it should keep most games competitive. The luck should also turn somewhat. A team whose differential implies 2.6 wins and has lost every close game should win a few coin flips from here. The offense is the cap. Its protection and passing numbers are bottom-of-the-league against every kind of defense, and only a healthy Alt, Harris and McConkey plus a less conservative plan would change that.

The schedule offers openings: Houston and the Jets at home, a Miami team at 1-5, and Tampa Bay and Las Vegas, both under .500. It closes with San Francisco, Kansas City and Denver, and the middle has Baltimore and New England. Expect a handful of wins built on defense and turnovers, scoring that stays in the mid-to-high teens, and points allowed that ease a little if the giveaways do.
swingFactors: Joe Alt's health and the line's pass protection
Whether the staff loosens the run-heavy plan

confidence.note: Six games, but the offensive collapse is consistent across opponents; injury returns add uncertainty.
